Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) -- Heavy rains smashed through a dam near Indonesia's capital Friday, unleashing a torrent of water that plowed into hundreds of homes and killed at least 52 people in what some survivors described as a suburban "tsunami." Members of a search and rescue team look for bodies around upended trees and vehicles near  Jakarta Friday. Sleeping residents were taken by surprise by the powerful flash flood as it crashed through Jakarta's crowded Cirendeu suburb, in the early hours of the morning. Rescue crews suspended their search for survivors overnight Friday evening, the National Disaster Coordination Agency said. The agency put the death toll at 52 with 17 missing. It said 33 people were injured and 1,490 left homeless. The Indonesian Health Ministry put the death toll higher at 58 people. After the deluge, drenched, injured and shivering survivors took refuge on the rooftops of their homes as rescuers in rubber boats struggled to reach them. Social affairs spokesman official Mardjito, who like many Indonesians goes by one name, said relief efforts were being hampered by debris from the dam. "We're still trying to get into the houses, but the problem is, mud is getting in our way," he said. Pictures from the scene showed the pulverized ruins of wooden buildings emerging as brown muddied waters subside.  Watch scenes of the flood devastation » . Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, currently on the campaign trail ahead of elections later this year, said he had ordered senior ministers to visit the scene of the disaster. "On behalf of the government, I express my condolences to the families of the dead victims and may their souls be accepted by God almighty," he said, according to the official Antara news agency. The rain obliterated a 255-meter-long section of the dam at around 4 am local time, releasing a wall of water from the 20-hectare lake that some survivors said reminded them of the tsunami that hit Indonesia in 2004. "They said they had heard loud rumbling sounds like during a powerful earthquake. They later found out that the sounds came from the water rushing out from the dam's lake," Antara said. Survivors told stories of dead relatives and harrowing brushes with death as they struggled to escape rising waters. Dewi Masitoh, a 40-year-old housewife, told the AFP news agency that she escaped with her husband and two daughters after they saw rising water reach the door of their stilt house. "We were on the second floor but my daughter went back downstairs when the window broke and water gushed in. My husband jumped in and pulled her out of the water by her neck. "I punched a hole through the roof and we all climbed up through," she said, showing cuts and scratches on her arms." Floods from heavy rains are an annual occurrence around Jakarta, a low lying city on the northern coast of Java island, where poor infrastructure often results in polluted canals and rivers spilling their banks and spilling into thousands of homes. In 2007, 38 people were killed and 430,000 forced from their homes when storm waters three meters deep in some places swamped 75 percent of the capital, which is home to about 9 million people. With poor sanitation and a hot and humid climate, the risk of water-borne diseases is usually a major concern following floods in the city, where mosquito-transmitted malaria is also a threat. CNN's Andy Saputra contributed to this report.

As the sprawling mega-metropolis of Southeast Asia, **Jakarta** serves as the political, economic, and cultural heart of **Indonesia**. With a population of over ten million people—and more than thirty million in its greater metropolitan area—Jakarta is a city of striking contrasts. High-rise glass skyscrapers stand alongside historic Dutch colonial architecture, and bustling street markets thrive just blocks away from luxury shopping malls. In this dynamic environment, global media networks like **CNN** play a crucial role in bringing the stories of Indonesia to the world, while also delivering international news to a local audience.

CNN’s relationship with Indonesia took a major leap forward with the launch of *CNN Indonesia* in 2015. Headquartered in Jakarta, this joint venture between Trans Media and Warner Bros. Discovery brought the global news brand's signature reporting style to the Indonesian archipelago. Broadcasting in Bahasa Indonesia across TV and digital platforms, CNN Indonesia has become a trusted household name, covering everything from domestic politics and economic shifts to local culture and sports.

From a global perspective, Jakarta frequently features in international CNN coverage as a bellwether for Southeast Asia's future. The capital city is at the center of several critical global narratives:

1. **Climate Change and Urban Planning:** Jakarta has frequently made headlines on CNN International due to its environmental challenges. Recognized as one of the fastest-sinking cities in the world due to land subsidence and rising sea levels, Jakarta’s plight spurred the Indonesian government's ambitious plan to move the national capital to Nusantara in East Kalimantan. CNN’s investigative pieces have highlighted both the human cost of flooding in Jakarta and the massive engineering effort behind the new capital project.

2. **Economic Dynamics and Politics:** As the powerhouse of Indonesia’s economy—the largest in Southeast Asia—Jakarta is where major financial policies and political movements unfold. CNN regularly reports on Indonesia's democratic elections, international summits like ASEAN, and the nation's rising status as a global economic player driven by tech innovation and natural resources.

3. **Culture and Travel:** It’s not all hard news. *CNN Travel* frequently shines a spotlight on Jakarta’s vibrant food scene and rich heritage. From street food favorites like *Nasi Goreng* and *Soto Betawi* to the historic alleys of Kota Tua (Old Town), CNN’s feature reporting captures the warmth and resilience of the people of Jakarta, known locally as *Warga Jakarta*.

As Indonesia continues to assert itself on the global stage, Jakarta remains the central arena where its future is forged. Through the lens of CNN, the world gets a front-row seat to the energy, challenges, and incredible transformation of Indonesia's vibrant capital.

**JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN)** — At least 58 people have been killed and more than 100 remain missing after a dam collapsed near Indonesia’s capital early Friday morning, sending a colossal wall of water crashing through sleeping residential neighborhoods, emergency officials said.

The disaster occurred around 2:00 a.m. local time in the Tangerang district, southwest of Jakarta, following days of torrential monsoon rain. The sudden breach of the century-old earthen dam unleashed an estimated 2 million cubic meters of water, inundating hundreds of homes under up to 20 feet (6 meters) of murky, debris-filled water.

Military personnel, police, and local volunteers are racing against the clock, using rubber boats and their bare hands to dig through thick mud and shattered timber in search of survivors.

### "It Sounded Like a Jet Engine"

For residents in the affected suburb of Cirendeu, the breach came with virtually no warning. 

Dewi Masitoh, a 34-year-old local resident, recounted the harrowing moment the floodwaters breached her home while her family was asleep. 

"I heard a loud roaring sound, like a low rumble of thunder that just wouldn't stop—it sounded like a jet engine," Masitoh said, speaking from a makeshift emergency clinic where she was being treated for minor cuts and shock. "Within seconds, the water smashed through our front door. It was completely black, and the current was terrifyingly fast."

Masitoh managed to scramble onto her roof carrying her six-year-old son, where they huddled in the pouring rain until rescuers arrived hours later. "People were screaming in the dark, calling out for their children, but then the voices were just washed away. We lost everything."

Local hospitals report being overwhelmed with victims suffering from trauma, hypothermia, and respiratory issues caused by inhaling muddy water. Emergency centers have been established in nearby mosques and school buildings to shelter more than 1,500 displaced residents.

### President Yudhoyono Pledges Full State Support

Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono arrived at the scene on Friday afternoon to assess the damage and oversee the emergency response efforts. Visibly shaken by the destruction, the President promised immediate state assistance for the victims and announced an urgent review of the country’s infrastructure.

"This is a profound national tragedy," President Yudhoyono told reporters while standing near the muddy basin of the breached dam. "Our immediate, absolute priority is saving lives, locating the missing, and providing adequate shelter and medical assistance to the displaced."

Addressing growing concerns over infrastructure safety, Yudhoyono ordered a nationwide audit of aging dams and water reservoirs. "We must determine why this structure failed. I have instructed the Ministry of Public Works to conduct a thorough investigation into the structural integrity of this facility to ensure such a catastrophe never happens again."

### A Megacity Built on Vulnerable Ground

Friday’s disaster highlights the chronic environmental and infrastructural vulnerabilities facing the Greater Jakarta area, a sprawling metropolis of over 10 million people.

Jakarta sits in a low-lying basin intersected by 13 major rivers and is plagued by severe seasonal flooding. The city's geography, combined with rapid, unregulated urban development, inadequate drainage systems, and massive groundwater extraction—which causes parts of the city to sink by up to 10 centimeters a year—makes it one of the most flood-prone urban centers in the world.

Major flood events in 2002 and 2007 previously paralyzed the capital, killing dozens and displacing hundreds of thousands of residents. However, officials noted that the sudden failure of a dam presents a far more lethal risk than the slow-rising river floods the city typically endures.

The dam involved in Friday's breach was originally constructed during the Dutch colonial era to manage local irrigation and reservoir levels. Environmental experts have long warned that many of the region’s older reservoirs are ill-equipped to handle the increasingly intense rainfall patterns linked to seasonal monsoons and global climate shifts.

### Rescue Efforts Continue Under Threat of Rain

With Indonesia’s meteorology agency predicting further heavy rainfall over the weekend, authorities fear that ongoing search-and-rescue operations could be hampered by additional flooding and landslides. 

Rescuers are continuing to search for the more than 100 people reported missing by distraught relatives, though officials privately acknowledge that the chances of finding more survivors diminish as the hours pass.

*CNN's Jakarta bureau contributed to this report.*

The disaster occurred around 4:30 a.m. local time when a structural section of the Cirendeu Reservoir Dam gave way under unprecedented water pressure. An estimated three million cubic meters of muddy water plunged into the densely populated river basins below while most residents were still asleep.

Within minutes, quiet residential neighborhoods were transformed into torrents of raging water, mud, and heavy debris.

"It sounded like a jet engine, and then the whole earth started shaking," said Agus Santoso, 42, a resident of the heavily hit Kampung Muara district. "I grabbed my children and ran to the roof. When I looked back, the entire street was just gone. I saw cars floating like toys and whole houses crushed. It wasn't just a flood—it was a wall of black water moving at terrifying speed. It was a tsunami."

By Tuesday afternoon, Indonesia’s National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) confirmed at least 34 fatalities, though officials warned the casualty count is expected to rise sharply. More than 70 people remain missing, and search-and-rescue teams are working frantically to locate survivors trapped beneath collapsed walls and thick layers of sludge.

Another survivor, 29-year-old Siti Rahayu, recalled the terrifying speed of the deluge. "The water surged from ankle-deep to over my head in less than two minutes," she said, cradling her toddler at an emergency relief center. "People were screaming from their roofs, waving flashlights in the dark. It carried the same destructive force as the images you see of sea tsunamis. Everything in its path was pulverized."

Footage broadcast by local television stations showed chaotic scenes of destruction. Massive trees were ripped from the ground, shipping containers were swept kilometers downstream, and power lines dangled dangerously over flooded streets. Heavy excavators and rubber dinghies operated by Basarnas, Indonesia’s national search and rescue agency, navigated through a sea of debris to pull stranded victims from upper-floor balconies.

Jakarta, a megacity of over 10 million people, is chronically prone to flooding during the annual rainy season. However, officials acknowledged that the sudden collapse of upstream infrastructure created a localized scenario far more violent than typical seasonal inundation.

"The structural integrity of the retaining wall was overwhelmed by an unprecedented volume of runoff after 48 hours of continuous torrential rain," said BNPB spokesperson Abdul Muhari during a press briefing. "Our immediate priority is saving lives, providing medical care to the injured, and securing the remaining perimeter of the dam to prevent further drainage."

More than 6,000 displaced residents have been evacuated to makeshift shelters set up in local mosques, university gymnasiums, and government buildings. Emergency workers are racing to supply clean drinking water, blankets, and medical supplies to prevent the outbreak of waterborne diseases.

The Indonesian Meteorological, Climatological, and Geophysical Agency (BMKG) has warned that heavy rainfall is expected to persist across the Greater Jakarta region for the next three days, raising fears of secondary landslides and impeding rescue efforts as nightfall approaches.
